# Results — Study 478 (Percentage Price Oscillator)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a bullish
PPO crossover (the PPO line rising above its 9-EMA signal) is a buy** — encoded as a mechanical
rule. PPO = 100·(EMA12 − EMA26)/EMA26, signal = 9-EMA of PPO; a long fires the first bar the PPO
crosses strictly above its signal, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we
measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **1082** mechanical bullish PPO crossovers pooled across the 5 tapes (12/26/9) |
| Timing / costs | PPO & signal read on the close of *t*; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per crossover |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — PPO crossover vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch crossover-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = crossover − random.

| horizon | n | crossover | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (cross−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 1080 | +21.6 bps | 59% | +3.08 | +35.8 bps | **−14.2 bps** | +19.6 bps | −1.41 | 0.159 |
| 10-day | 1080 | +45.0 bps | 61% | +4.08 | +69.9 bps | **−24.9 bps** | +43.0 bps | −1.71 | 0.088 |
| 20-day | 1078 | +90.3 bps | 63% | +5.98 | +154.0 bps | **−63.6 bps** | +88.3 bps | **−3.13** | 0.002 |
| 60-day | 1072 | +280.3 bps | 69% | +7.86 | +324.7 bps | **−44.4 bps** | +278.3 bps | −1.31 | 0.190 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+5.98** at 20 days,
**+7.86** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index
inherit the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the PPO crossover is *worse* at
**every** horizon (Δ = −14.2 / −24.9 / −63.6 / −44.4 bps), and at 20 days it is *significantly*
worse (Welch *t* = **−3.13**, *p* = 0.002 — the wrong sign of "significant"). The crossover does
not forecast; it actively under-times relative to a coin flip.

## Does normalizing MACD add edge? (the third-axis question)

The PPO is MACD divided by the slow EMA — the same crossover machinery, scaled to a percent. We
run the **raw MACD** crossover (12/26/9, no division) on the identical tape and compare each to
the same random baseline.

| horizon | PPO Δ (vs random) | raw-MACD Δ (vs random) | difference |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | −14.2 bps | −12.0 bps | −2.2 bps |
| 10-day | −24.9 bps | −23.8 bps | −1.1 bps |
| 20-day | −63.6 bps | −68.9 bps | +5.3 bps |
| 60-day | −44.4 bps | −52.3 bps | +7.9 bps |

The two are **statistically indistinguishable** — both lose to random by essentially the same
margin at every horizon. Normalizing the spread changes the *units* of the oscillator, not the
*timing* of its crossovers (a monotonic rescaling by a slow-moving EMA barely moves where
PPO − signal changes sign). The normalization buys **comparability across instruments**, not
**edge**. Thesis: **Busted**.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the crossover loses to random everywhere

| ticker | entries | crossover | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (cross−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 227 | +75.1 bps | +2.65 | +156.2 bps | **−81.1 bps** |
| QQQ | 210 | +128.2 bps | +3.82 | +192.0 bps | **−63.8 bps** |
| IWM | 216 | +86.6 bps | +1.93 | +162.5 bps | **−75.9 bps** |
| DIA | 218 | +90.1 bps | +3.33 | +145.9 bps | **−55.8 bps** |
| GLD | 211 | +72.9 bps | +2.05 | +113.3 bps | **−40.4 bps** |

The crossover *underperforms* a dart-throwing entry in **5 of 5** names — there is no instrument
where the normalized crossover beats random. The healthy one-sample *t*'s are all drift.

## Crossover placebo — scramble the sign structure, nothing improves

The decisive "does the crossover structure matter?" test: keep the *marginal* of |PPO − signal|
(so crossings happen about as often) but permute which bars sit above vs below the signal line,
so the specific up-crossings become noise. If the real crossover were carrying timing
information, the real result would sit in the right tail of the scrambled distribution.

| test | observed PPO-crossover 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-sign crossover | +75.1 bps | **0.998** | 500 |

**99.8% of scrambled-sign crossovers match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.998) — the real PPO
crossover is one of the *worst* timed entries in the scrambled cloud. The specific crossover
structure carries no useful information.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real continuation

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-crossover continuation (knob `edge`), the same PPO
crossover rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing
there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | crossover | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no continuation) | 166 | +41.9 bps | 58% | +1.09 |
| **0.60** (real planted continuation) | 70 | +1224.3 bps | 99% | **+19.21** |

With no planted continuation the control sits at *t* ≈ 1.1 (no false positive at the *t* ≥ 2
bar); a real planted continuation lights up at *t* = +19.21 with a 99% win-rate. The detector is
live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The PPO crossover does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (crossover − random = −14.2 / −24.9 / −63.6 / −44.4 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the Welch *t* is
  **negative** at every horizon and *significantly* so at 20 days, **−3.13**, *p* = 0.002). The
  impressive one-sample *t*'s (20-day +5.98, 60-day +7.86) are pure beta — the upward drift of
  long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed; in fact the crossover *under-times* relative to random, and costs only deepen the
  hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more fully by holding the index.
- **Does normalizing MACD add edge? — BUSTED.** The raw MACD crossover and the normalized PPO
  crossover lose to random by statistically indistinguishable margins at every horizon, and the
  shuffled-sign placebo leaves the result intact (*p* = 0.998). Normalization changes the
  oscillator's *units*, not its *timing* — it buys cross-instrument comparability, not forecasting
  power.
